answers.answer: The API producer publishes the export job ID and inputs. The broker holds the job; confirmed broker acceptance under the configured durability rules permits a truthful accepted response with the job ID and pending status. A worker receives the job, renders and saves the file and ready status, then acknowledges processing so the broker can retire that delivery. The saved required file makes ready truthful; neither publisher confirmation nor consumer acknowledgement alone proves it. Users check status and must see failed if processing terminates unsuccessfully. The login decision must remain synchronous because granting access requires its final result first. One added operating cost is tracking job status after the original request ends. No unsupported step is needed.

evidence.quote: Publishes a message containing the job ID and inputs. An API must confirm the handoff before telling the client the job was accepted.
A publisher confirmation means broker acceptance under the configured durability rules, not completed application work.
Receives the message, saves the required result and ready status, then acknowledges processing to the broker.
Return a job ID and make pending, ready and failed status observable; ready means the required result has actually been saved.
Authorization must finish before granting access to a private resource; queueing that decision cannot justify granting access immediately.
The trade-off includes operating the broker and workers, tracking status, handling duplicates and retries, and watching backlog.

answers.answer: With at-least-once delivery, the broker may redeliver the already-credited job because its acknowledgement was not received. Acknowledging first could retire the delivery and lose the credit if the worker crashed before saving it. Reuse one stable business-operation ID for all retries. In a single database transaction, insert it into a durable processed-jobs table with a unique constraint and apply the balance credit; commit both or neither. A duplicate ID skips the credit. A separate check followed by a write could race or crash between steps. This protects the database effect from duplicates, not universal exactly-once delivery or atomic external effects. No unsupported step is needed.

evidence.quote: A worker commits its database changes, then crashes before acknowledging. With at-least-once delivery, the broker can deliver the job again. Acknowledging first instead risks losing the work if the worker crashes before saving it.
Reuse a stable business-operation ID across retries, not a new ID per attempt.
In one database transaction, insert that ID into a durable processed-jobs table with a unique constraint and apply the job's database effect. Commit both or neither. A duplicate ID skips the effect.
That transaction protects its database effects. It does not make an external email or payment atomic, or turn delivery into a universal exactly-once guarantee.

answers.answer: Retry the temporarily unavailable image store with increasing delays and a finite attempt or time budget. Immediate retries could deepen the outage. Once the budget is exhausted, isolate the job in a dead-letter queue for investigation and expose failed status. Isolate the unsupported-format job without waiting for retries to cure it: waiting will not make that format supported. Isolating failures lets healthy jobs continue. Before deliberate replay, fix the cause and check whether an earlier attempt already applied an effect; retain duplicate safety during replay. The lesson does not specify numeric delays or a numeric budget, so those values remain unsupported here.

evidence.quote: A temporary storage outage may recover. Retry with increasing delays and a finite attempt or time budget; immediate retries can deepen the outage.
An unsupported input format will not improve with waiting. Isolate it, or any job that exhausts its budget, in a dead-letter queue for investigation and expose failed status.
Healthy jobs can continue. Before deliberately replaying a failed job, fix its cause and check whether an earlier attempt already applied an effect. Replay still needs duplicate safety.

answers.answer: The second write can set quantity to 2, then the slower first write can overwrite it with 5, leaving the wrong final quantity of 5. Ordered receipt does not order completion or effects. Serialize effects by item ID: later updates for that item wait while the earlier update runs or retries. Different items may execute concurrently, but one busy item becomes a throughput bottleneck. If the earlier job is isolated, repair or cancel it before releasing dependent updates; isolation alone does not resolve their dependency. No unsupported step is needed.

evidence.quote: Delivery order and completion order are different.
Workers receive them in order, but the slower old update finishes last and overwrites new.
Serialize effects per entity ID: keep later updates waiting while an earlier one runs or retries. Different entities can still run in parallel. A busy entity becomes a throughput bottleneck.
Moving the earlier job to a dead-letter queue does not resolve the dependency. Decide how to repair or cancel it before releasing dependent updates.

answers.answer: Backlog grows by approximately 120 - 80 = 40 jobs per second while those rates continue. Increasing oldest-job age shows that jobs are waiting longer and the promised delay may be violated. Bound worker concurrency at the image store safe limit. Apply producer backpressure by throttling or rejecting new requests with a visible busy response, or explicitly deferring within an agreed limit. Queue buffering has finite storage and retention; it absorbs a burst only if capacity later catches up before those limits or the allowed delay are reached. More workers help only when workers are the bottleneck and downstream services have spare capacity; the stated image-store limit means adding concurrent downstream work is not the remedy here. Applying the lesson downstream-capacity rule to the image store uses the supplied scenario; no additional mechanism or numeric limit is supported.

evidence.quote: If 100 jobs arrive each second and 70 finish, unfinished work grows by 30 jobs per second. Watch backlog and oldest-job age: a growing wait can violate the promise to the client.
Storage and retention are finite. A queue can absorb a burst only if capacity later catches up before those limits or the allowed delay are reached.
Bound worker concurrency to protect the database. Throttle or reject new requests with a visible busy response, or explicitly defer them within an agreed limit.
More workers help when workers are the bottleneck and downstream services have spare capacity.

answers.answer: One work queue divides jobs among competing workers, so placing billing and analytics among those workers does not give each application every purchase event; failures can still cause repeat delivery. A retained log with separate billing and analytics groups lets each application independently read every retained purchase event and maintain its own progress. A partition is an ordered slice of the log; each group tracks an offset for each partition, and workers within a group share partitions. Committing an offset records progress without deleting the event. Analytics can rewind and replay the last day only if all required events still remain under the retention policy when replay occurs. More partitions or consumers do not change the lesson guarantees: order is per partition, not global, and retained history and offsets do not themselves make external effects exactly once. The lesson supplies no extra mechanism that would establish either stronger guarantee.

evidence.quote: A work queue divides jobs among competing workers; it does not give every independent application every job. Failed deliveries can still repeat.
A retained log keeps event history for consumers to read independently. If billing and analytics each need every purchase event, separate consumer groups can track their own progress.

In Kafka, a partition is an ordered slice of the log. Each group tracks its own position, called an offset, for each partition. Workers within a group share the partitions. Committing an offset records progress; it does not delete the event.

A group can rewind and replay only while the required events remain under the retention policy. Ordering is per partition, not global. Retained history and offsets do not by themselves make external effects exactly once.
